title: Lyme disease reached high incidence in northern US counties below the 2800 degree-day tick limit in 2002-2017; distance to infected counties, not local warming, set the time of spread
abstract: Question: did the spread of Lyme disease into US counties follow the climate limit for Ixodes scapularis establishment of Ogden et al. (2005; about 2800 C-days above 0 C per year), and did local warming change when counties became endemic? Method: a pre-registered county hazard analysis. We used CDC county case counts 2001-2019, Census populations and daily CPC 0.5-degree temperature (checked against 16 stations: 49 C-days low, anomaly r 0.96). A county emerged in the first year of a 3-year run at 10 or more cases per 100,000. The domain was 1,432 counties north of 37 N and east of 100 W, in two regions (Northeast, Midwest). The model had year effects, distance to the nearest endemic county, a degree-day climate spline and a past 3-year degree-day anomaly, with a future-anomaly placebo and county-cluster bootstrap. An independent check used New York nymph surveillance 2008-2025. Results: 342 counties emerged in 2002-2017. Distance controlled the timing: half the distance gave 3.8 times the annual odds. Near endemic counties, cool counties emerged at least as fast as warm ones (Northeast 13% vs 10% per year; Midwest 9% vs 4.5%), and 16 of 30 counties below the limit emerged, 11 of 24 when we used the warmest grid cell in the county. A breakpoint was not identified (2900 C-days, 95% interval 2350-3600). The past warming term was near zero: -0.04 log-odds per 100 C-days (-0.14 to 0.06); both regions and both periods agreed. The pooled placebo was positive, but it became zero with region-by-year effects. In New York, nymphs occurred in the coolest county in 5 of 13 years, the degree-day gradient of nymph density decreased after 2016 and infection prevalence did not change with degree-days. Limitations: cases are by county of residence, small counties need few cases, the grid is coarse, and we did not test hosts or forest.

display.caption: Year of Lyme disease emergence (first year of a 3-year run at 10 or more cases per 100,000) in 1,432 northern US counties. Black: high incidence at the start (2001-2003). Grey: no emergence by 2017. Red rings: counties with 1991-2000 CPC degree-days below 2750 C-days (the CPC equivalent of the 2800 station limit). Many ringed counties in Maine, New Hampshire, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan emerged.

Left: annual emergence probability of at-risk counties within 100 km of an endemic county, by 1991-2000 degree-days (bins of 200 C-days with 15 or more county-years, 95% binomial intervals). Probability does not fall below the Ogden limit (dashed); it falls in warm Midwest counties. Right: profile likelihood of the hinge breakpoint; the curves are flat within 2 log-likelihood units in the Midwest and pooled data, so the data do not identify a limit.

Left: effect of the past 3-year degree-day anomaly (blue) and of the future anomaly placebo (grey) on annual emergence log-odds, with 95% county-cluster bootstrap intervals, for the frozen samples, sensitivity runs and exploratory region-by-year models. Right: New York nymph density against county degree-days in 2008-2016 and 2017-2025; the gradient became flatter as cool counties gained ticks.

citations.reason: Source of the about 2800 C-day establishment limit that we tested with county Lyme disease emergence.
Uses the degree-day limit to project northward range expansion with warming; our data show spread below the limit and no warming effect on timing at county scale.
County-scale I. scapularis distribution; context for spread from endemic foci.
Earlier campaign use of the same NYSDOH nymph data as a forecast test of density; we add the degree-day limit and Lyme emergence tests.
